blocks.html:
Saving languages

The campaign to keep minority languages alive

Paragraph A (Q27):

A Ten years ago, Michael Krauss, a professor at the University of Alaska, shocked his colleagues in the discipline of linguistics with his prediction that half the 6,000 or so languages spoken in the world would disappear within a century. Krauss founded the Alaskan Native Language Center to preserve as much as possible of the 20 tongues still known to the state's indigenous people. Only two of those languages were being taught to children, and the rest were rapidly falling from use. Other linguists are making similar predictions. A survey in Australia found that 70 of the surviving 90 Aboriginal languages were no longer used regularly by all age groups. The same is true for all but 20 of the other 175 North American languages in the US.

Paragraph B (Q28):

B Outwardly, the consolidation of human language might seem like a good trend that could ease ethnic tensions and aid global commerce. Linguists don't deny those benefits, and they acknowledge that small communities often choose to switch to the majority language because they believe it will boost their social or economic status.

Paragraph C (Q29):

C Many experts in the field nonetheless mourn the loss of rare languages, for several reasons. Some of the most basic questions in linguistics have to do with the limits of human speech, still far from fully explored. Many researchers would like to know which elements of grammar and vocabulary—if any—are universal. An English researcher, Nicholas Ostler, offers an example: 'Ica, spoken in northern Colombia, seems to have nothing comparable to a personal pronoun system—I, we, you, etc. Otherwise, I would have thought that personal pronouns were a linguistic universal.' Other scientists try to reconstruct ancient migration patterns by comparing borrowed words in otherwise unrelated languages. In each of these cases, the wider the range of languages you study, the more likely you are to get the right answers.

Paragraph D:

D 'I think the value is mostly in human terms,' says James Matisoff, a specialist in rare Asian languages at the University of California. ‘Language is the most important element in the culture of a community. When it dies, you lose the special knowledge of that culture and a unique window on the world. But despite the constant talk about saving endangered languages over the past ten years, the field of descriptive linguistics has accomplished little in this respect. You would think that there would be some organised response to this situation, some attempt to determine which languages can be saved and which should be documented before they disappear,' says Sarah G. Thomason, of the University of Michigan. ‘But there isn't any such effort.'

Paragraph E (Q30):

E However, there are some signs of progress. The Volkswagen Foundation, a German charity, has created a multimedia archive in the Netherlands that can house recordings, grammars, dictionaries and other data. Contributions from the Ford Foundation have helped a master-apprentice programme, in which fluent speakers receive $3,000 to teach a younger relative their native tongue through shared activities. So far, about 75 teams have completed the programme. ‘It's too early to call this language revitalisation,' admits Leanne Hinton of Berkeley. ‘In California, the death rate of elderly speakers will always be greater than the recruitment rate of young speakers. But if nothing else, we prolong the survival of the language.' This will give linguists more time to record these tongues before they vanish.

Paragraph F (Q31):

F Complicating matters, dozens of institutions around the world are setting up digital libraries on endangered languages. This could create chaos, because the projects use non-standardised data formats, terminology and even names of languages. Gary F. Simons, of the Dallas-based research group SIL International, has been working to bring some order to this by building an ‘open languages data community'—a kind of digital card catalogue. This system will allow researchers to check their theories against a vast array of data.

Paragraph G (Q32):

G However, even if a language has been fully documented, all that remains once it vanishes from use is a fossil skeleton. Linguists may be able to sketch an outline of the language and fix its place on the evolutionary tree, but little more. As yet, there is no discipline of conservation linguistics. Almost every strategy to keep people speaking a language has succeeded in some places but failed in others. One factor that always seems to occur in the death of a language, according to Hans-Jurgen Sasse of the University of Cologne in Germany, is that speakers start regarding their own language as inferior to the majority language. Children pick up on the attitude, and prefer to speak the dominant language. This is how Cornish and some dialects of Scottish Gaelic slipped into extinction.

Paragraph H (Q33):

H 'Ultimately, the answer to the problem of language extinction is multilingualism,' argues James Matisoff. ‘Even uneducated people can speak a number of languages if they start as children.' Many people in the world are at least bilingual, and in some places it is common to speak three or four languages. But in addition to the fact that children may reject minority languages, there is also the concern that speakers of a majority language may react badly to speakers of minority languages. The first step in saving dying languages may be to persuade the world's majorities to allow the minorities among them to speak with their own voices.

meta.title: Saving languages 拯救濒危语言

passageNotes.label: Paragraph A
passageNotes.text: 十年前，阿拉斯加大学的教授迈克尔·克劳斯（Michael Krauss）震惊了语言学界的同事们，他预测世界上约6000种语言中有一半将在一个世纪内消失。克劳斯创立了阿拉斯加原住民语言中心，以尽可能保存该州原住民仍然知晓的20种语言。其中只有两种语言正在教授给儿童，其余的正在迅速停止使用。其他语言学家也做出了类似的预测。澳大利亚的一项调查发现，现存90种原住民语言中有70种不再被所有年龄段的人经常使用。美国其他175种北美语言中，除了20种之外，情况也是如此。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph B
passageNotes.text: 从表面上看，人类语言的整合似乎是一个好趋势，可以缓解种族紧张局势并促进全球贸易。语言学家并不否认这些好处，他们承认小型社区通常选择转向多数语言，因为他们认为这将提升他们的社会或经济地位。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph C
passageNotes.text: 尽管如此，该领域的许多专家仍然为稀有语言的消失而感到惋惜，原因有几个。语言学中一些最基本的问题与人类言语的极限有关，这些极限远未被充分探索。许多研究人员想知道语法和词汇中的哪些元素——如果有的话——是普遍存在的。英国研究员尼古拉斯·奥斯勒（Nicholas Ostler）举了一个例子：哥伦比亚北部使用的伊卡语（Ica）似乎没有任何类似于人称代词系统的东西——我、我们、你等。否则，我会认为人称代词是一种语言普遍现象。其他科学家试图通过比较不相关语言中的借词来重建古代迁徙模式。在每一种情况下，你研究的语言范围越广，你就越有可能得到正确的答案。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph D
passageNotes.text: 加州大学稀有亚洲语言专家詹姆斯·马蒂索夫（James Matisoff）说：我认为价值主要体现在人文层面。语言是社区文化中最重要的元素。当它消亡时，你就失去了该文化的特殊知识和了解世界的一个独特窗口。但是，尽管过去十年来关于拯救濒危语言的讨论不断，描写语言学领域在这方面取得的成就甚微。密歇根大学的萨拉·G·托马森（Sarah G. Thomason）说：你会认为会有一些有组织的应对措施，一些尝试来确定哪些语言可以被拯救，哪些应该在消失之前被记录下来。但是没有任何这样的努力。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph E
passageNotes.text: 然而，也有一些进展的迹象。德国慈善机构大众汽车基金会在荷兰创建了一个多媒体档案馆，可以容纳录音、语法、词典和其他数据。福特基金会的捐助帮助了一个师徒计划，在该计划中，流利的说话者获得3000美元，通过共同活动教年轻亲属他们的母语。到目前为止，大约75个团队已经完成了该计划。伯克利大学的利安妮·欣顿（Leanne Hinton）承认：现在称这为语言复兴还为时过早。在加州，老年说话者的死亡率将始终高于年轻说话者的招募率。但至少，我们延长了语言的存活时间。这将给语言学家更多时间在这些语言消失之前记录它们。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph F
passageNotes.text: 使问题更加复杂的是，世界各地数十个机构正在建立关于濒危语言的数字图书馆。这可能会造成混乱，因为这些项目使用非标准化的数据格式、术语甚至语言名称。总部位于达拉斯的研究组织SIL国际的加里·F·西蒙斯（Gary F. Simons）一直致力于通过建立一个开放语言数据社区——一种数字卡片目录——来为此带来一些秩序。这个系统将使研究人员能够根据大量数据来检验他们的理论。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph G
passageNotes.text: 然而，即使一种语言已经被完整记录下来，一旦它从使用中消失，剩下的只是一具化石骨架。语言学家或许能够勾勒出语言的大致轮廓，并确定其在进化树上的位置，但仅此而已。迄今为止，还没有保护语言学这一学科。几乎每一种让人们继续说某种语言的策略在某些地方成功了，但在其他地方失败了。德国科隆大学的汉斯-尤尔根·萨斯（Hans-Jurgen Sasse）认为，在语言消亡过程中似乎总是出现的一个因素是，说话者开始认为自己的语言不如多数语言。孩子们会注意到这种态度，并倾向于说主导语言。康沃尔语和苏格兰盖尔语的一些方言就是这样走向灭绝的。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph H
passageNotes.text: 詹姆斯·马蒂索夫认为：归根结底，语言消亡问题的答案是多语制。即使是未受过教育的人，如果从小开始，也能说多种语言。世界上许多人至少会说两种语言，在某些地方，会说三到四种语言是很常见的。但是，除了孩子可能会拒绝少数语言这一事实之外，还存在多数语言的说话者可能对少数语言的说话者反应不佳的担忧。拯救濒危语言的第一步可能是说服世界上的多数群体允许他们中的少数群体用自己的声音说话。
